title: Q: Why does temperature approach but never mathematically reach the surrounding temperature?
notes: The solution θ − θ₀ = (θ₁ − θ₀)·e^(−Kt/mc) is an exponential decay — it approaches zero asymptotically as t → ∞, but never equals exactly zero for any finite time

Physically, as θ gets very close to θ₀, the driving temperature difference (θ − θ₀) shrinks toward zero, so the rate of heat loss also shrinks toward zero — cooling effectively stalls near room temperature well before the math says it's 'finished'
The solution θ − θ0 = (θ1 − θ0) e^(−t/τ) is positive for every finite t if the body starts above room temperature. An exponential e^(−t/τ) reaches zero only in the limit t → infinity.
So the mathematical temperature never becomes exactly θ0 at a time you can write down. It gets as close as you like if you wait long enough.

The physical reason is in the rate equation itself. The rate of fall is proportional to the remaining excess. As the excess shrinks, the rate shrinks, so the last part of the fall takes longer and longer.
After a few time constants the excess is a few percent of the start. A thermometer may not resolve it, and the body is then called 'at room temperature' for practical purposes.
confusion: 'Never' means never at a finite time, not that the body stays hot.
The asymptote is θ0, not zero Celsius.
A small unmeasured difference is not a contradiction of the formula.
The rate does not stay at its initial value.
keyPoints: The exponential is zero only at infinite time.
The driving excess shrinks as the body cools.
In practice the difference becomes too small to measure.

exercises.question: τ = 10 min and the initial excess is 40°C. Find the excess at t = 10 min and say whether the body is at room temperature.
steps: At t = τ the factor is e^(−1) ≈ 0.37.
The body is still 15°C above the room.
It is not at room temperature. That would require the exponential to be zero.
exercises.answer: About 15°C of excess remains. The body has not reached the room.

summary: Under Newton's law the excess temperature decays exponentially and is zero only after an infinite time. The rate slows as the excess shrinks, so the temperature approaches the room and a thermometer eventually cannot tell the difference.
